extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theory, lawmakers, and legal/political thinkers
extracted.subtask_short: limits on legislative and executive power
extracted.subtask_description: Normative criteria about the legitimacy, limits, and proper exercise of legislative, executive, and federative powers in a commonwealth — covering consent, promulgation, property, separation of powers, representation, prerogative, and the people's residual sovereignty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law must rest on the consent of the society
rubrics_metrics.description: No body can have a power to make laws over a society except by the society's own consent and by authority received from them; obedience ultimately terminates in this supreme power and is directed by laws which it enacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any claim that a prince or foreign power can bind members of a society against the community's consent is rejected. Laws not publicly approved by the society lack the lawful power of making them; without consent, lawmaking is mere tyranny (see Hooker citations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative power is not absolutely arbitrary over lives and fortunes
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislative can be no more than the power individuals had in the state of nature and is limited to the public good; it cannot have a right to destroy, enslave, or designedly impoverish the subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because no one can transfer more power than he has, the community's legislature cannot claim absolute arbitrary authority over persons or property. The law of nature remains an 'eternal rule' to which human laws must conform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislature must govern by promulgated standing laws and known judges
rubrics_metrics.description: The supreme authority cannot rule by extemporary arbitrary decrees but is bound to dispense justice and decide rights by promulgated standing laws and known authorized judges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relying on unwritten law leaves rights uncertain; standing laws and authorized judges prevent private misapplication of the law, protect property, and avoid every person being 'judge, interpreter, and executioner' in their own case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human laws must conform to the law of nature (and God)
rubrics_metrics.description: Human laws and rules must be conformable to the law of nature (the will of God as its declaration); no human sanction can be valid against the fundamental law of preservation of mankind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislators are constrained by higher moral/ natural law standards; laws contrary to these are 'ill made' and not properly binding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws should be general rules, not varied in particular cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws are to be promulgated established laws, 'not to be varied in particular cases,' so there is one rule for rich and poor alike.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniform, general rules allow citizens to know their duties and secure their rights; ad hoc variations undermine security and the limits on rulers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary end of laws: the public good
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws ought to be designed for no other end ultimately than the good of the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative acts are fiduciary and must be judged by whether they preserve and promote the community's safety, peace, and prosperity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxes and takings require the consent of the people
rubrics_metrics.description: The supreme power cannot take from any man any part of his property without his own consent; it must not raise taxes on the property of the people without the consent of the people given by themselves or their deputies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Property preservation is an end of government; unilateral claims to tax or seize property without consent 'invade the fundamental law of property' and subvert government purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislature cannot transfer its lawmaking power to others
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislative, being a delegated power from the people, cannot pass the power of making laws over to any other hands; the people alone can appoint who shall make laws for them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because legislative power is a positive voluntary grant, it cannot be alienated by legislators to other bodies or private hands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subordinate/ministerial offices hold only delegated authority and are accountable
rubrics_metrics.description: Other ministerial and subordinate powers in a commonwealth have no authority beyond what is by positive grant and commission delegated to them, and are all accountable to some other power in the commonwealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative and subordinate powers are not independent sovereigns; their legitimacy depends on explicit delegation and they remain subject to oversight and removal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative supremacy while government subsists, but subject to people's residual power
rubrics_metrics.description: While government subsists the legislative is the supreme power within the commonwealth, yet the people retain a supreme power to remove or alter the legislative when it acts contrary to the trust reposed in them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The legislative's supremacy is fiduciary; if it betrays the public trust or opposes the ends of government, authority reverts to the people who may reconstitute governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: People retain right to resist force without authority (state of war)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using force upon the people without authority and contrary to trust is a state of war with the people, who have the right to reinstate their legislative in the exercise of its power; the remedy of force without authority is to oppose force to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the executive prevents convening the legislature when constitution or public exigency requires it, the people may lawfully resist; illegitimate force makes the aggressor liable to be treated as at war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation: legislative ideally distinct from executive to prevent abuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Because it may be a temptation to grasp power, it is dangerous for the same persons to make laws and execute them; in well-ordered commonwealths the legislative power is put into hands distinct from those who execute the laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separation ensures rulers remain subject to laws they enact and reduces the risk they will suit law and execution to private advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of a standing executive power (always in being)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no need that the legislative should be always in being, but it is absolutely necessary that the executive power should be always in being, because laws require perpetual execution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The executive's continuity is justified by the constant need to enforce and administer laws; however, this power remains ministerial and (normally) subordinate to the legislature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive's convoking/dissolving power is fiduciary, not superiority
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of assembling and dismissing the legislative, placed in the executive, gives not the executive superiority over it, but is a fiduciary trust placed in him for the safety of the people, to be exercised only for the public weal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convocation prerogatives exist because fixed rules cannot anticipate all exigencies; yet their use must be guided by the public good and not private will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive/federative power discretion for matters affecting foreigners is necessarily flexible
rubrics_metrics.description: The federative power (war and peace, leagues and alliances) is less capable of being directed by antecedent standing positive laws and must be left in great part to the prudence and wisdom of those who manage it for the public good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because dealings with foreigners depend on variable external circumstances, rigid prior rules are impractical; discretion is required but should be exercised for public advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation must remain proportionate and remediable when corrupted
rubrics_metrics.description: Over time representation may become unequal or disproportionate; this injustice needs remedy, and measures that restore fair and equal representation are justifiable as for the public good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The executive may, in the interest of the public and true representation, regulate numbers of representatives where old custom has produced gross absurdities (e.g., rotten boroughs). Whatever rectifies representation toward the public interest is 'just prerogative.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerogative: executive discretion to act for public good, including mitigation and pardon
rubrics_metrics.description: The executive has a discretionary power (prerogative) to act according to the public good where the municipal law gives no direction, and in some cases even against it — e.g., mitigating severity of the law or pardoning offenders when preservation of the whole demands it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prerogative exists because legislators cannot foresee every accident; it permits necessary, time-sensitive action for preservation of the society, but must be exercised for public advantage, not private gain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislature may resume execution powers and punish maladministration
rubrics_metrics.description: When the legislative has put the execution of laws into other hands, they retain the power to resume it and to punish for any maladministration against the laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delegation of executive duties is revocable; legislative oversight and the ability to remove or punish maladministration are essential checks on delegated executives.
